newsitem.title: USA: Israel offers to negotiate -- but what?.
newsitem.headline: Israel offers to negotiate -- but what?.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu arrived for an emergency summit in Washington promising to put an end to a burst of Middle East violence through non-stop talks with the Palestinians.

But his limited offer -- to negotiate a long-delayed Israeli pullback from Hebron, the last and most sensitive of seven occupied West Bank cities -- will ring hollow for Palestinians who already have an internationally recognised deal on Hebron with the Jewish state signed a year ago.
Netanyahu's offer will also anger his critics who accuse him of being more interested in a peace process -- with the emphasis on process -- rather than real peacemaking.
The 46-year-old Israeli leader of the right-wing Likud party opposes swapping occupied Arab land for peace -- the policy that is the bedrock of five years of U.S.-backed Middle East talks.

When he came to power 15 weeks ago on a vow to bolster Israeli security after a wave of suicide bombings, Netanyahu inherited the Hebron deal along with the rest of a Palestinian self-rule accord he viewed as fundamentally flawed.

On Sunday, after four days of Israeli-Palestinian gunbattles that claimed 72 lives, Netanyahu's adviser David Bar-Illan said it was "clear as day" that Palestinian President Yasser Arafat would now have to accept a substantial change in the Hebron agreement.

It remains to be seen how Netanyahu, meeting Arafat on Tuesday for only the second time, can renegotiate Hebron while keeping a separate promise to adhere to Israel's international commitments. It is as much a challenge for him as for U.S. President Bill Clinton at Tuesday and Wednesday's summit to uphold good U.S.-Israeli relations and prevent a collapse of Arab-Israeli ties.

The United States, Israel's greatest strategic asset but also the main sponsor of Middle East peace talks, could lean on Netanyahu to set a deadline for completing a handover. But Clinton's time and ability to push may be limited with the U.S. presidential election five weeks away.
Aides to Netanyahu reject deadlines as "artificial" in any event.

Netanyahu is counting on overwhelming popular support in Israel for a hard line because of the clashes, unprecedented in three years of Israeli-PLO peace moves, which took the lives of 15 Israeli soldiers along with 57 Palestinians.
Israelis were outraged by the bloodshed, accusing Arafat's 30,000-strong police force of turning the very weapons against them that had been issued to Palestinians because of the peace deal.

Palestinians blamed last week's outburst on the slow pace of peacemaking and a pedestrian tourist tunnel Netanyahu opened near a Moslem shrine in Jerusalem on one of the most religiously sensitive pieces of real estate in the world.
Arafat demands the tunnel opening be closed, but the tunnel was the one issue Netanyahu said on Monday would definitely not be on the summit agenda.

If Netanyahu renegotiates Hebron, he will boast to Israelis that he clinched a better deal for the 400 Jews living there surrounded by 100,000 Arabs than did his Nobel peace laureate predecessors Yitzhak Rabin and Shimon Peres.
Almost exactly a year ago, at the last Washington summit on the Middle East, Rabin and Peres sealed the deal with Arafat, promising to pull back from Hebron by March 1996.

Then in February and March, Islamic suicide bombers killed 59 people in attacks against Israel. Peres, in a tight election race for prime minister against Netanyahu, put off the Hebron handover. Peres lost the election and Hebron has been on hold ever since.

Flying to Washington, Netanyahu told reporters the round-the-clock talks, starting immediately, would also focus on easing a more than seven-month-old West Bank and Gaza Strip closure and letting Palestinians run a Gaza airport.
But here too Palestinians will ask: Why these issues?

The closure was never considered a negotiating issue. Netanyahu already has committed to easing the closure, raising the number of Palestinians allowed to work in Israel from 22,000 to 37,000 and promising to raise it to 50,000.

And while the airport, a paved strip in the Gaza desert, is a matter of prestige, its importance to Palestinians pales in comparison to overdue negotiations on further Israeli pullbacks and talks on difficult "final-status" issues such as the future of Jerusalem, Jewish settlers and statehood.
Netanyahu refuses to cede on any of these issues, due to be resolved by May 4, 1999, setting the stage for deadlock.
